extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, students, and historians
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for the practice of public relations and publicity—what constitutes effective, ethical PR, the role of the public relations counsel, and techniques for informing and adjusting to publics. Emphasizes professional duties, use of social science methods, distinction from press agentry, and examples of practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity as social control / first step to solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity 'stands as the first step in its solution' for abuses and is broad enough to allay suspicion; 'the making public, both to the government authorities and to the public at large, the essential facts in which the public is concerned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance from Henry C. Adams and Theodore Roosevelt: disclosure should be as broad as the ground of suspicion, and 'the mere fact of the publication would cure some great evils, for the light of day is a deterrent to wrong-doing.' Use publicity to inform both government authorities and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing the public and building goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations activities should be used to 'stimulat[e] the interest of the public in an individual or organization, and building goodwill.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: institutional advertising (Bell System), companies carrying on informative publicity (telephone company, railroads), and non-profits (YMCA). Use releases, newsreels and films to inform and build public favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid whitewash/press agentry; prefer truthful dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity that is merely 'whitewash' or 'press agentry' is distinguished from dissemination that leads to reform; much PR was 'merely the now-familiar whitewash.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion is honesty/transparency—do not use PR to cover wrongdoing. The profession should emphasize information and reform over fake or manipulative promotion; examples of negative publicity practices (space-grabbing, propaganda) are cited as anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel role vs. press agent role
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations counsel should not be limited to 'get[ting] pieces in the newspapers' or acting as a press agent; instead they should advise clients on policies and practices conforming to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel's function includes recommending policy changes and management adjustments, not merely securing media coverage. Critiques of early PR show the profession must transcend press agentry and become advisory and policy-oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social science and tested techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is 'the body of theory and technique utilized in adjusting the relationships of a subject with its publics' and represents applications of sociology, social psychology, economics and political science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practice should draw on social sciences and specialized skills (journalism, advertising, organizational expertise). Employ established theoretical frameworks and tested techniques rather than ad hoc tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze maladjustments and locate probable causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A public relations counsel is an expert in 'analyzing public relations maladjustments; locating probable causes of such maladjustments in the social behavior of the client, and in the sentiments and opinions of publics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should diagnose relationship problems between client and publics, identify root social or behavioral causes, and target interventions to those causes rather than treating symptoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise on suitable social theories and tested techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel should 'advise the client on suitable social theories and tested techniques in solving many of the problems of society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations should be theory-informed and evidence-backed. Counsel must translate social science and prior experience into practical policy and communications measures for clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way activity: policy formation and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Good public relations is a 'two way activity — proper policy formation and interpretation to the public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR requires both internal change (policy formation responsive to public interest) and external communication (interpreting policy to publics). Firms that view PR as only outward publicity fail this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good PR equals good performance publicly appreciated
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortune's formulation: 'good . . . public relations is good performance — publicly appreciated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure PR success by the client's actual conduct and the public's recognition of that conduct, not by amount of media coverage or promotional noise alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid propaganda and space-grabbing (use facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propagation and manipulative 'propaganda' (space-grabbing, offering bribes to opinion leaders) are condemned; organizations like the NELA limited themselves 'to facts and figures about the industry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factual, verifiable information rather than manipulative or deceptive messaging. Anti-patterns include paid manipulation of opinion leaders and propaganda campaigns intended to mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scientific public-opinion research
rubrics_metrics.description: The public opinion poll (e.g., Gallup) emphasized 'a scientific approach to questions of what the public really thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate polls and empirical research to understand publics' attitudes; base strategy on measured opinion rather than assumptions or anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization: ethics, training, and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession needs clarification, 'the development of ethical concepts and the licensing and registration of practitioners as in other professions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build formal ethics, university training, continuing education, and possible licensing/registration to raise standards and accountability in PR practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align organization policies with public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations develops from the concept that 'public and private interest coincide' and organizations must 'modify its attitudes and actions to conform to public demand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR success requires substantive policy alignment with public expectations, not merely rhetorical adjustment. Use PR to facilitate organizational change toward public-interest concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and objectivity of counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent counsels had advantages: 'more objective judgment, direct access to top executives and greater prestige' compared with inside PR staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising clients, maintain objectivity and sufficient access to leadership to influence policy; recognize tradeoffs between inside staff and independent firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness from advertising and sales promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is distinct from 'sales promotion, publicity and press agentry' and should not be confused with advertising agencies' public relations departments simply diverting fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear role definitions: PR focuses on relationship management and public interest adjustment, while advertising focuses on commercial promotion. Beware of conflating the two in practice and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select appropriate media and techniques for public education
rubrics_metrics.description: PR employs varied vehicles—press releases, institutional advertising, newsreels, motion pictures, pamphlets, radio scripts—to 'inform the public' and shape understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match medium to audience and message (e.g., U.S. Steel's technicolor motion picture to depict manufacturing). Use sustained, multi-channel campaigns when necessary to educate and adjust public attitudes.
